A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original attack-success, image-quality, human-evaluation, KL-estimation, and sample-selection experiments in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and reports additional evaluations using ConvNeXT and adversarially trained ResNet-50 in Appendix Q.

M1.justification: The adversarial distribution in Equation 3, SDXL/LoRA augmentation, diffusion-model fitting, and conservative/aggressive sample selection remain unchanged. The expanded concept definition and newly disclosed sampling settings do not establish an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate identity-preserving targeted attacks using the same 26 DreamBoothPlus concepts and 30 ImageNet target classes. Additional classifiers change model configurations, while the new advertising and physical-patch scenarios are discussed without corresponding experiments.

E2.justification: NCF is added to the existing MobileNet V2 and ViT-Base attack and image-quality comparisons in v2 Tables 11–12 and 16–17; it was absent from the corresponding v1 Tables 7–10. The main comparison set remains NCF, ACA, DiffAttack, and ProbAttack.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes the transfer-success criterion from top-100 to top-5. Appendix Q adds top-1/5/10 evaluations, ConvNeXT and adversarially trained ResNet-50 surrogate configurations, and a ResNet-50 Adv transfer target. The documented dataset sizes and fine-tuning budgets remain unchanged; Appendix P supplies previously unspecified settings.

E4.justification: Appendix Q extends robustness testing to direct white-box attacks on adversarially trained ResNet-50, beyond the earlier transfer evaluations against defended models. Appendix I adds comparative runtime analysis. The sample-selection sensitivity study and qualitative case studies are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: The common-random-number KL estimator and its mean/variance reporting are retained, including identical uncertainty values. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for attack performance.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive top-1/5/10, new-surrogate, image-quality, and runtime results, while omitting the former complete top-100 comparisons. Matched white-box values also change: MobileNet V2 OURS rises from 97.18% to 97.31%, and ViT-Base ProbAttack from 63.33% to 63.85%. The main ResNet-50 white-box results and Table 2 are unchanged. Top-5 and top-100 rates are not directly comparable.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 changes from a Gaussian variance result in v1 Section 3.2 to a general Gibbs-distribution result in v2 Section 3.4. Appendix A replaces the proof with a derivation showing that the KL derivative with respect to inverse temperature equals the difference in expected distances. Theorem 2 and the KL-estimation derivations remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The introduction adds practical guidelines and application scenarios to the explicit contribution list. The central claims about concept-preserving adversarial generation, higher attack success, and consistency with probabilistic attacks remain substantively unchanged in the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: New Appendix H explains weak transferability through differing victim distributions and proposes an identity-preservation tradeoff. Appendices I and K–L add model-collapse considerations, application scenarios, and mitigation discussions. The new assertion of consistently best transferability is overbroad: Table 10 reports VGG19 top-1 success of 1.15% for OURS (AGGR), versus 1.67% for DiffAttack. The original limitations paragraph is relocated, not newly added.

D1.justification: V2 adds an explicit project URL and descriptions of reproducibility resources. Table 9 documents DDPM sampling with 250 steps and c = 30, alongside baseline sampling budgets, attack steps, and step sizes. Appendix I expands runtime reporting to baseline fine-tuning and per-image generation costs. These are substantive documentation additions, without evidence that the retained procedures changed.

R1.justification: Section 6 substantially expands positioning through AdvGAN, AdvDiffuser, AdvDiff, NatADiff, and perceptual attacks. New Table 3 distinguishes single-image, identity-level, and class-level capabilities. Additional transferability literature supports Appendix H, extending the earlier discussion centered on Song et al. and ProbAttack.

P1.justification: The concept explanation is substantially rewritten into separate concept-distribution and distance-distribution subsections, and related work is restructured. Main-text limitations and usage guidelines move to Appendices O and K, while the former additional-experiments appendix becomes Appendix Q. New ethics and reproducibility statements further reorganize the document.

P2.justification: V2 adds the transferability schematic in Figure 6 and new positioning, runtime, and settings tables. Appendix results are reorganized into multi-metric tables with additional comparator columns and surrogate configurations. Existing qualitative image examples are retained, alongside extensive conference-template and layout changes.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens justification and reproducibility through the broader conditional theorem and proof, explicit top-1 transfer results, stricter evaluation metrics, defended-surrogate tests, and previously missing sampling and baseline settings. These address important gaps in v1. There are shortcomings: Appendix Q promises top-100 results that its tables omit, and the new transferability discussion overstates consistent superiority. Nevertheless, the gains in theoretical scope, empirical transparency, and reproducibility documentation provide a substantial net improvement.
